text:
Winamp isn’t pulling the numbers out of thin air. The audio file gets decoded into raw PCM samples, and the visualiser plugin is handed those samples in chunks as playback proceeds. For the spectrum display, the samples are fed through a fast Fourier transform. That converts the time-domain waveform into frequency-domain amplitude, so each column corresponds to a frequency bin. The height of each column comes from the bin magnitude, scaled to fit the window. This is the same basic idea as any spectrum analyzer: you take a block of audio, estimate its frequency content, and draw it.
The oscilloscope part is simpler. It plots the actual sample values over time, essentially drawing the waveform you get after decoding. So when you see the classic green bars or line, you are looking at live measurements from the audio stream, not a pre-rendered video. That matters because the picture changes with the music: quiet passages give low peaks, heavy bass makes the low-frequency bins jump, and a sudden drum hit shows up as a sharp spike.
One detail worth noting is that the transform has to be done often enough that the display feels live, so the visualisation runs continuously during playback. In older Winamp versions this was handled by a dedicated visualiser component that the output plugin feeds. The actual rendering is just 2D drawing into the window; nothing here requires 3D or a fancy GPU pipeline. The look people remember comes from the display settings, the bin layout, and how the amplitudes are smoothed and scaled, not from any hidden picture.
Practically, the FFT has to use a window function so that one short block of samples doesn’t leak its edges into nearby bins. Winamp also applies smoothing and peak-hold so a fast transient doesn’t make the display flicker uselessly. The vertical scale can be linear or logarithmic, which is a lot of the reason the same audio can look different in different skins or visualiser presets. It is the same audio, just presented differently. You can see the mechanism in the options: a larger FFT size means narrower frequency resolution but slower response to changes. In practice, the visible differences between presets are mainly scaling, smoothing and frequency layout, and how bins are grouped. That is the core idea here, not a separate video effect. The audio buffer is the source of truth for what you see.
